messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
The standard error (i.e., the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null) is  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}} \approx 0.22 .
\]
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely means the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis. The standard error is sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size). But they mention "standard deviation of the null hypothesis test" maybe they want the standard error of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null. That is sigma/sqrt(n). They gave sample_std_dev=1.4, sample_size=40. So SE = 1.4 / sqrt(40) = 1.4 / 6.3249 = about 0.2215. So answer ~0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic under null is sqrt((n-1)/n)? Actually t-statistic has distribution t_{n-1}. But the standard deviation of t distribution is sqrt(df/(df-2)) for df>2. Here df=39, so sd = sqrt(39/37) ≈ sqrt(1.05405)=1.0268. But that's not typical. Usually we talk about standard error of mean.

Given context: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6." They might want the standard error of the mean difference: sqrt((sd^2/n)+(pop_sd^2/N)). But population sd unknown. They only give sample sd. So likely standard error of sample mean: 1.4/sqrt(40).

Thus answer: 0.2215.

We can also compute t-statistic: (98.2-98.6)/(1.4/sqrt(40)) = -0.4/0.2215 = -1.805. But they didn't ask for t-statistic.

Thus answer: 0.2215.

We should respond with the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test: 0.2215. Probably round to 0.22.

Thus answer: 0.22.
